cards.text: This one's a psalm of the sons of Korah, written for the choirmaster. It opens by calling people to hear this and listen. Friend, that's somebody tapping a spoon on a glass, and the WHOLE room goes quiet.

cards.question: The writer wants people to hear this. How far does his call to listen reach?

answers.text: Everyone in the world rich and poor alike
Everyone in Israel from the least to greatest
The rich and the powerful in every land

cards.text: Then the writer says his mouth will impart wisdom, and the meditation of his heart will bring understanding. He'll turn his ear to a proverb and express his riddle with the harp.
So here's the riddle. In times of trouble, when wicked usurpers surround him, why should he be afraid?

cards.question: The wicked usurpers surrounding the writer are leaning hard on something. What do they trust in?

cards.text: They trust in their wealth and boast in their great riches. Never had that problem myself, friend, because my WHOLE price tag was 25 cents.

cards.question: True or false: with enough money, a man can redeem his brother by paying his ransom to God.

cards.text: The redemption of a soul is costly, and no payment would ever be enough. That's a bill even the guy who mentions his boat in EVERY conversation can't cover.

cards.question: No payment could ever be enough to redeem a soul. What would that payment be trying to buy?

answers.text: A seat in the king's own court

cards.text: Now look around, friend. The writer says it's clear that the wise man and the fool end up the same way.

cards.question: The writer says it's clear that wise men ___ just like the foolish and the senseless.
When the foolish and the senseless perish, what happens to all their wealth?

cards.text: Some of these folks even had their lands named after them. The Millers, the family whose kitchen I worked in, carved my name on my handle, and I STILL ended up in the back of a junk drawer.

cards.question: The writer speaks of people whose lands were named after them. He says their ___ are their eternal homes.
True or false: the writer says that despite his wealth, a man cannot endure.

cards.text: All that wealth, and he still can't endure. The writer says he's like the beasts that perish.
The writer keeps going: "This is the fate of the foolish…" Then the psalm marks a Selah.

cards.question: True or false: the writer says the fate of the foolish is not shared by their followers who endorse their sayings.

cards.text: Then he paints a picture, and it gets DARK. The foolish are like sheep, destined for Sheol.

cards.question: The foolish are like sheep destined for Sheol. Who does the writer say will be their shepherd?
True or false: the writer says the foolish will rule over the upright in the morning.

cards.text: Their form will decay in Sheol, far from their lofty abode. Then the writer drops one little word that flips the whole psalm: But.

cards.question: The foolish are headed for Sheol. So who does the writer say will redeem HIS life from Sheol?
True or false: the writer says God will surely take him to Himself.

cards.text: That line gets me EVERY time, friend, because the Most High sent an angel to call me out of a dark junk drawer. Then the writer gives some advice about a man whose house keeps getting fancier.

cards.question: The writer says not to be ___ when a man grows rich and the splendor of his house increases.
So why shouldn't you be afraid when a man grows rich?

answers.text: When he dies he carries nothing away
His riches will soon be stolen from him
He will lose it all before he grows old

cards.text: His abundance will not follow him down. Every last bit of it stays behind.
In his lifetime he blesses his own soul, and the writer adds that men praise you when you prosper. Land ONE promotion, friend, and people who haven't texted you in YEARS suddenly want to catch up.

cards.question: The rich man blessed his own soul in his lifetime. But when he dies, who does he join?

cards.text: And that generation of his fathers will never see the light of day.

cards.question: In the last line, the man who is like the beasts that perish is the one with riches but without ___.
